analysis.one_liner: Bans betting on U.S. political elections and contests on regulated trading platforms.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on the last days of the 118th Congress with no cosponsors and died in committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal commodities law to make it illegal for any regulated exchange to list or clear bets on the outcome of political elections or contests. The aim is to keep election results from becoming a financial market, where large wagers could create incentives to distort campaigns or undermine public trust in vote counting. It was introduced in the final days of a two-year Congress and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters benefit from rules that keep elections from becoming a venue for high-stakes gambling, which election officials and regulators have warned could create incentives to influence outcomes or shake confidence in results. Candidates and election workers also benefit from a lower risk of financial markets attached to their races.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits any agreement, contract, transaction, or swap based on a political election or contest from being listed or cleared on a regulated exchange, amending the Commodity Exchange Act's anti-gambling provisions [S2].

By routing the ban through the Commodity Exchange Act, it targets the same section of law that governs wagering contracts on regulated trading venues, closing a channel through which election betting reached mainstream markets [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Prediction market platforms and their traders lose the ability to offer and take election-related bets on regulated exchanges. Traditional sportsbooks and offshore betting sites are already restricted or unregulated in this area, so the main direct cost falls on licensed event-contract venues.

drawbacks.text: Some defenders of prediction markets argue that election markets aggregate information and can be more accurate forecasts than polls, and that banning them pushes this activity to offshore, unregulated sites where no oversight exists [S2].
The bill addresses only contracts listed on regulated venues; it does not by itself reach illegal offshore betting, so its practical effect on total election gambling may be limited [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is narrow and well-targeted: it closes a specific legal channel for election gambling without touching ordinary financial markets. The main trade-off is that banning regulated election markets may push some wagering to unregulated offshore sites, and some analysts value prediction markets for forecast accuracy. Against that, keeping elections out of the betting markets protects public confidence in results, which most voters would likely judge worth the cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in the final week of the Congress, and the committee never acted before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Merkley introduced the bill on December 20, 2024, less than three weeks before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, which has jurisdiction over commodities law [S4].
No cosponsors signed on and no further action was taken before the Congress expired [S3][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Prediction market platforms keep their ability to offer election-related contracts, and no one who wanted election gambling restricted got anything; the proposal died without attracting any cosponsors.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the final week of the 118th Congress

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over the Commodity Exchange Act
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; the bill died in committee when the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No votes or recorded positions exist; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors, and died quietly in committee.

industries.note: The bill strips regulated platforms of election and political contest contracts, a popular and profitable product line. Their revenue from election betting depends on making election outcomes a tradable financial market, which the bill treats as a threat to election integrity.

Licensed sportsbooks are largely barred from election wagering already, so the ban mostly doesn't change their position; offshore operators lose nothing because the bill only reaches regulated exchanges. The main effect is to keep a betting category from migrating into mainstream regulated venues.
